book: How Search Decides What You See
author: Aaron Tay

episodes.title: Two questions. One search.
episodes.subtitle: Relevance, precision, recall, and candidate boundaries

scenes.title: Useful to whom?
scenes.claim: Relevance depends on the person, purpose, and situation
scenes.narration: A tiny paper arrives at our cosmic library. A researcher needs its method. A beginner needs an overview. A reviewer excludes it under the review's criteria. One paper, three defensible verdicts. Chapter fourteen asks how to measure retrieval. First, we must write down what useful means for this particular task.

scenes.title: A score is an estimate
scenes.claim: Metrics score agreement with recorded relevance judgements
scenes.narration: The chapter separates four perspectives: the system's estimate, whether the paper is about the topic, whether it informs this reader, and whether it helps accomplish this task. These are a teaching simplification. A high similarity score is not the judgement itself. Every metric inherits the relevance criteria and judgements it receives.

scenes.title: Two fractions. Different questions.
scenes.claim: Precision: relevant / retrieved    •    Recall: retrieved relevant / all relevant
scenes.narration: In the chapter's controlled example after reranking, ten displayed records include six judged relevant. The entire collection contains exactly ten relevant records. Precision at ten is six divided by ten displayed records. Recall at ten is six divided by ten relevant records. Both are sixty percent here, but their denominators count different things.

scenes.title: A deeper net catches more
scenes.claim: Along a fixed ranking, recall cannot fall; precision can rise or fall
scenes.narration: Lowering a cut-off can recover more relevant records and increase screening work. Along a fixed ranking, recall cannot decrease, while precision can rise or fall. This is not an unavoidable trade between systems: a better ranking can improve both at the same depth. A quick lookup and an evidence review also value different errors.

scenes.title: Where did the denominator come from?
scenes.claim: Known-seed recovery and relative recall do not establish absolute recall
scenes.narration: In a live database, nobody normally knows every relevant record. Recovering three out of four known seeds measures seed recovery. Comparing against judged-relevant records in several strategies' pooled union measures relative recall. Both are useful checks. Neither reveals the true total. Ask where a reported recall denominator came from.

scenes.title: Better order. Same twenty records.
scenes.claim: Figure 14.1: precision@10 and recall@10 rise from 0.2 to 0.6
scenes.narration: Now watch the chapter's twenty-record pool. Before reranking, only two relevant papers appear in the first ten. After reranking, six do. Precision at ten and recall at ten both rise from point two to point six. All ten relevant papers were already candidates. Candidate-pool recall stays one hundred percent throughout.

scenes.title: Ranking cannot rescue an excluded paper
scenes.claim: A fixed candidate set creates a recall ceiling for downstream stages
scenes.narration: Suppose a relevant paper never became a candidate. Shuffling the existing cards cannot bring it through the boundary. A careful reranker can improve ordering, and a generous display cut-off can expose more candidates. Neither operation creates a new candidate. A good ranking of an incomplete pool can still be a poor search.

scenes.title: Cross the boundary with a new retrieval
scenes.claim: Additional routes or rounds help recall only by finding new relevant records
scenes.narration: A fresh query, another source, a hybrid route, or another search round can expand the cumulative candidate pool. In this schematic example, a new relevant card raises recovery; a duplicate or irrelevant card does not. More candidates can also push useful records below the display cut-off. Measure candidate coverage and displayed results separately.

scenes.title: Position changes what gets seen
scenes.claim: Set membership alone cannot describe a good ranking
scenes.narration: Two search engines return the same papers. One puts the useful paper first; the other puts it tenth. Precision and recall over the whole set cannot see this difference. People can. Ranked retrieval needs measurements that reward useful records appearing where a reader is likely to notice them.

scenes.title: Precision@10: count the first page
scenes.claim: Equal relevant counts inside the cut-off give equal precision@10
scenes.narration: Precision at ten counts judged-relevant records among the first ten results. These schematic lists each have two, so both score point two. It does not care whether the hits occupy ranks one and five, or eight and ten. At rank eleven, a record contributes nothing to precision at ten.

scenes.title: MRR: how soon is the first hit?
scenes.claim: Reciprocal rank = 1 / first relevant rank; MRR averages across queries
scenes.narration: Reciprocal rank asks where the first relevant result appears. At rank two, the score is one half. At rank five, one fifth. Mean reciprocal rank averages those scores across queries: point three five for these two examples. It fits known-item tasks, but ignores every useful record after the first hit.

scenes.title: MAP: reward many early hits
scenes.claim: Average precision uses precision at each relevant hit, divided by all relevant records
scenes.narration: Average precision rewards many relevant records placed high. In this complete toy judgement set, three records are relevant. For hits at ranks one, three, and five, average the precisions at those positions: one, two thirds, and three fifths. The result is about point seven five six. M A P averages average precision across queries.

scenes.title: nDCG: grade usefulness, discount distance
scenes.claim: Higher grades and earlier positions contribute more; normalise by the ideal order
scenes.narration: Normalised discounted cumulative gain accepts grades of relevance. A common convention turns grade three into gain seven, and grade one into gain one, then discounts gain by rank. Divide by the ideal ordering's score. Our fully judged toy list scores about point nine eight three with the strongest record first, and point five nine zero with it third.

scenes.title: Three good papers can repeat one aspect
scenes.claim: Conventional relevance metrics do not explicitly reward new aspect coverage
scenes.narration: Even graded relevance can miss another problem. Three individually useful papers may all discuss the same aspect. A task may need methods, implementation, and limitations together. Conventional n D C G does not explicitly reward that coverage. Diversity-aware metrics need aspect judgements and an additional definition of what a useful set should cover.

scenes.title: Three depths can have three jobs
scenes.claim: Evaluation depth, retrieval boundary, and reranker budget are independent choices
scenes.narration: Keep the depths separate. A retriever might return one hundred candidates, a reranker inspect forty, and an evaluator judge the first ten. These are illustrative budgets, not recommended settings. The k in precision at k names evaluation depth. It need not equal the retrieval boundary or the reranker's candidate budget.

scenes.title: Choose the metric that fits the task
scenes.claim: Quoting a metric chooses a definition of better
scenes.narration: Ask what better should mean. A useful first page suggests precision at a fixed depth. One correct item suggests mean reciprocal rank. Many early hits suggest mean average precision. Graded usefulness suggests normalised discounted cumulative gain. All require recorded judgements. A metric is a choice about the task, not a universal quality stamp.

episodes.title: Build a test your library owns
episodes.subtitle: Benchmarks, local judgements, and hidden regressions

scenes.title: Hold three things still
scenes.claim: A test collection fixes documents, queries, and relevance judgements
scenes.narration: To compare retrieval systems, build a little laboratory. Hold the document collection, the queries, and the relevance judgements still. Run both systems against those same conditions. This is the core of the Cranfield approach to offline evaluation. User studies and task-based evaluations answer complementary questions about what people actually accomplish.

scenes.title: Unjudged does not mean irrelevant
scenes.claim: Pooling can penalise useful records outside the judged pool
scenes.narration: Judging every document for every query rarely scales. Evaluators often pool the highest-ranked results from several systems and judge their deduplicated union. A common scoring convention treats unjudged items as non-relevant. If a different system finds a useful record outside that pool, it can be penalised. Missing judgement is not evidence of irrelevance.

scenes.title: A leaderboard belongs to its test
scenes.claim: Transfer depends on collection, language, document types, topics, and criteria
scenes.narration: A benchmark establishes performance on its collections, topics, and assessors' criteria. It does not automatically establish performance on your chemistry theses, your non-English holdings, or your researchers' actual questions. Use benchmark results as evidence about that comparison. Then test whether the gain survives the conditions your library cares about.

scenes.title: Start with real needs and known failures
scenes.claim: Thirty to fifty queries is a practical starting range, not a completeness guarantee
scenes.narration: The chapter suggests thirty to fifty real queries as a practical starting range. Take them from reference enquiries, search consultations, training, and interlibrary loans. Include known failures deliberately. Record the information need, relevance criteria, and known useful records. Building and judging the set can take much longer than rerunning an established baseline.

scenes.title: Pool both runs; judge to one depth
scenes.claim: Fixed depth + shared criteria + pooled judgements make runs comparable
scenes.narration: Choose a fixed evaluation depth, such as ten or twenty. Capture both runs, pool and deduplicate their results at that depth, and judge every pooled record against the same written criteria, ideally without seeing which run supplied it. Compute precision at that depth. Report seed recovery separately, and document the denominator when a run returns fewer results.

scenes.title: Plant four deliberate stress tests
scenes.claim: Test exact identity, indexed units, vocabulary mismatch, and opposite meanings
scenes.narration: Plant four probes. An exact identifier tests identity. A phrase found only in held full text tests the indexed unit. A useful record sharing almost none of the query's words tests vocabulary mismatch. Two near-identical queries with opposite meanings test composition. Judge the opposite queries separately. Each probe gives a regression somewhere to reveal itself.

scenes.title: The average rises. A query collapses.
scenes.claim: Table 14.3: row mean 0.30 → 0.33, while identifier precision falls 0.3 → 0.1
scenes.narration: The chapter's hypothetical table hides a warning. Identifier precision falls from point three to point one. Vocabulary-mismatch precision rises from point two to point five. The composition row stays point four. The equally weighted mean of these three rows rises from point three zero to point three three. That third row already averages two separately judged queries.

scenes.title: Keep the rows, the baseline, and the evidence
scenes.claim: A metric identifies a difference; diagnosis and answer evaluation ask further questions
scenes.narration: Rerun the local set after model updates, index changes, migrations, and before renewal. Inspect per-query changes and run-to-run variation. A metric can identify a decline without explaining its cause. For generated answers, also check source support and faithfulness. A faithful summary of the wrong shortlist still inherits the retrieval failure. Keep the comparison inspectable.
